title: Chinese Braised Mushrooms
subtitle: Shiitake mushrooms braised in oyster sauce, dark soy, and sesame
excerpt: Dried shiitake mushrooms reconstituted and braised in oyster sauce absorb the braising liquid and turn glossy and rich. The soaking liquid is the secret -- it deepens the sauce considerably. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Braised shiitake mushrooms in oyster sauce (mo gu bao) appear in Cantonese home cooking and restaurant menus alike, and feature in classic texts including The Chinese Cookbook by Craig Claiborne and Virginia Lee (1972) as well as modern compilations of Hong Kong family cooking. Dried shiitake soaked and braised in their own liquor is a technique rooted in Chinese Buddhist vegetarian cooking, where the mushrooms serve as a primary source of umami.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The mushrooms can be braised up to 2 days ahead, stored in their sauce in the fridge, and reheated gently. The sauce thickens on standing -- add a splash of water when reheating.

content.text: This serves 4 as a side dish and takes about 50 minutes, of which 30 are passive soaking time. Dried
shiitake mushrooms
soaked in warm water release a deeply savoury liquid that becomes the base of the braising sauce. Using that liquid rather than discarding it is what gives this dish its intensity.

Leave a little headspace when adding the soaking liquid -- the last few tablespoons at the bottom of the bowl can carry grit from the dried mushrooms. Pour the liquid through a fine sieve if you want to be thorough. The braise takes only 15 minutes once the mushrooms are hydrated, and the sauce reduces to a dark, glossy glaze that coats the mushrooms thickly.
What you need
Method

Place the dried shiitake mushrooms in a bowl and cover with 400 ml of warm (not boiling) water. Leave to soak for 30 minutes until fully hydrated and soft. Remove the mushrooms, squeezing gently over the bowl to reserve the liquid. Trim off the woody stems and discard.
Strain 250 ml of the mushroom soaking liquid through a fine sieve into a jug, leaving any grit behind. Mix in the oyster sauce, dark soy sauce, light soy sauce, sugar, and Shaoxing wine.

Heat the vegetable oil in a saucepan or wok over medium-high heat. Add the ginger and garlic and cook for 30 seconds until fragrant. Add the soaked mushrooms cap-side down and press gently to ensure contact with the pan.

Pour in the seasoned soaking liquid. The liquid should come halfway up the mushrooms. Bring to a gentle simmer, then cover and braise for 10 minutes. The mushrooms will absorb the sauce and the liquid will reduce. The
dark soy sauce
turns the sauce a deep mahogany colour.

Remove the lid and increase the heat to medium-high. Stir the cornflour slurry and pour it into the simmering sauce, stirring constantly. The sauce should thicken within 30 seconds to a glaze consistency that coats the back of a spoon. Add a splash of water if it over-thickens. The
oyster sauce
gives the glaze a slightly caramelised, savoury sweetness.
Remove the ginger and garlic. Drizzle the
sesame oil
over the mushrooms and toss to coat. Transfer to a serving dish cap-side up and spoon the remaining glaze over the top. Serve immediately alongside steamed rice.

items.symptom: Sauce is too thin and does not cling
items.cause: Insufficient cornflour, or the slurry was added all at once without stirring
items.fix: Mix a little extra cornflour with cold water and add in a slow stream while stirring. Add in small increments until the right consistency is reached.

items.symptom: Mushrooms taste flat despite a dark sauce
items.cause: The soaking liquid was discarded, or mushrooms were soaked too briefly
items.fix: The soaking liquid carries most of the umami. Always use it as the braising base. Soak for the full 30 minutes in warm water.

items.cause: Soaking liquid was poured in without straining, carrying mushroom sediment
items.fix: Strain the soaking liquid through a fine sieve or a piece of muslin before using. Leave the last tablespoon in the bowl.

content.text: Where this dish lives

Braised shiitake mushrooms are a vegetarian staple in Chinese Buddhist cooking. They appear at New Year banquets as a symbol of longevity. The soaking liquid is full of flavour; use it in the braising sauce. Do not throw it away.
